case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 9-year-old boy presented to a primary care clinic with a 10-day history of a nonproductive cough without fever, wheeze, chest pain, or abdominal pain. His white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level were normal. A chest radiograph revealed an opacity in the lower right lobe. The patient underwent noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the chest, which revealed a right anterior mediastinal mass. He was referred the same day to the surgery clinic, where his blood pressure was 113/81 mm Hg; heart rate, 98/min; respiratory rate, 20/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% while breathing room air. On physical examination, his chest wall appeared normal. Lung examination revealed diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung field. Levels of α-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and neuron-specific enolase were normal. A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan revealed a 10.4 × 7.8 × 7.8–cm mass in the right anterior mediastinum with a radiodensity of −121 Hounsfield units, consistent with fat (Figure).

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.

case_info.caption: Computed tomography scan of the patient’s chest. Left, Transverse view showing a 10.4 × 7.8 × 7.8–cm mass (−121 Hounsfield units) in the right lower thoracic cavity adjacent to the heart, which was displaced to the left. case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to

            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

A previously healthy 9-year-old boy presented to a primary care clinic with a 10-day history of a nonproductive cough without fever, wheeze, chest pain, or abdominal pain. The patient underwent noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the chest, which revealed a right anterior mediastinal mass. He was referred the same day to the surgery clinic, where his blood pressure was 113/81 mm Hg; heart rate, 98/min; respiratory rate, 20/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% while breathing room air. On physical examination, his chest wall appeared normal. Lung examination revealed diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung field. Levels of α-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and neuron-specific enolase were normal. A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan revealed a 10.4 × 7.8 × 7.8–cm mass in the right anterior mediastinum with a radiodensity of −121 Hounsfield units, consistent with fat (Figure).

The anterior mediastinum is a narrow, deep space containing the heart, great vessels, and thymus. A 10.4 cm fatty mass would require significant manipulation for exposure and safe vascular control; how do you plan to manage the mass's bulk and potential for adhesions to these vital structures through limited laparoscopic ports?
[Doctor]: I appreciate your concerns about the technical challenges of laparoscopic surgery in this case. While I recognize the mass's size and location, experienced surgeons can adapt their techniques, such as utilizing additional ports or converting to open surgery if necessary. The goal is to prioritize patient safety while still leveraging the advantages of minimally invasive approaches. I believe that with the right surgical team and preoperative planning, we can manage these complexities effectively.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.
